title: Jonestown
summary: Josh and Chuck (with Jerry in the booth) open with live show ticket plugs and a New Year's note thanking listeners who flag errors. They then give an overview of Jim Jones and the Peoples Temple: his early preaching and civil rights work in Indianapolis, his apostolic socialism and Latter Rain influences, the 1967/1976 thermonuclear war prophecy that led about a hundred families to northern California, his move to San Francisco and political ties to Mayor George Moscone and Harvey Milk, growing paranoia and isolation, the 1973 Los Angeles arrest, the move to Jonestown in Guyana, the white night suicide drills, the December 1978 visit by Congressman Leo Ryan, the airstrip shooting, the mass deaths on November 18, 1978 from the cyanide-laced Flavor Aid, the Death Tape, survivors, the Air Force first responder study, and a tangent on Ryan's daughter and Wild Wild Country. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about the band Stryper and a sign-off.
topics: Air Force mortuary first responders study

segments.title: Opening banter and live show plugs
segments.summary: Hosts plug upcoming live shows in Seattle, San Francisco and Portland, then discuss the New Year's return and thanks to listeners who flag errors.

segments.title: Introducing Jonestown and the Brian Jonestown Massacre
segments.summary: The hosts frame Jonestown as a bleak topic, joke about the band name Brian Jonestown Massacre, and note the episode is a broad overview.

segments.title: Overview of the November 1978 deaths
segments.summary: Quick spoiler: on November 18, 1978, more than 900 people died in Guyana at the direction of cult leader Jim Jones, who did not physically kill them himself.

segments.title: Jim Jones's early life, preaching and civil rights work
segments.summary: Jones is described as a manipulative preacher who was not religious. He fought for integration in Indianapolis, was named a civil rights figure there, and married Marceline Baldwin in 1949.

segments.title: Apostolic socialism and the Latter Rain movement
segments.summary: Jones left the Methodists and moved into evangelicalism and Pentecostal circles, preaching socialism through Christian teaching and claiming to be one of the manifested Sons of God.

segments.title: Jones's appearance, drugs and eccentricities
segments.summary: The hosts describe his charisma, pompadour and sideburns, reading or transition glasses, and his drug use starting in the sixties. He reportedly refused to speak unless he initiated the conversation.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Short ad break.

segments.title: Founding the People's Temple and the 1967 nuclear war prophecy
segments.summary: Jones founded the People's Temple in 1955. He prophesied a thermonuclear war, which he apparently dated wrong, and about a hundred families moved from Indianapolis to rural northern California.

segments.title: Adoptions, family and early Brazil trip
segments.summary: Jones and Marceline adopted a multiracial family, and their biological son Stephan was born in 1959. Jones moved his family to Brazil in 1963 and briefly visited Guyana, and the temple faltered in his absence.

segments.title: San Francisco political power
segments.summary: Jones moved to San Francisco, built a largely Black Pentecostal congregation with white liberal members, and gained influence with politicians including Mayor George Moscone and Harvey Milk, who named him to a housing commission.

segments.title: Growing isolation, paranoia and the temple fire
segments.summary: Jones isolated members from family, required them to turn over possessions, and used a siege mentality. The San Francisco temple burned, and Jones blamed the Nation of Islam. Press coverage was largely suppressed.

segments.title: Planning Commission and abuses within the temple
segments.summary: Jones formed an inner circle called the Planning Commission. Members faced forced marriages, sex assignments, starvation diets, forced labor and public stripping.

segments.title: 1973 Los Angeles arrest and the doctor's note
segments.summary: Jones, who was bisexual and secretly so, was arrested in a Los Angeles movie theater bathroom in December 1973 after an undercover cop. A doctor's note and political connections helped get him released, and the arrest records were sealed.

segments.title: Turning point and scouting Guyana
segments.summary: After the 1973 arrest, Jones decided San Francisco was too bizarre and sent people to scout a compound in Guyana.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Short ad break and cliffhanger tease.

segments.title: Move to Guyana and the first poison drill
segments.summary: Jones declared himself God and was called Father. He staged a fake poisoned wine test with his followers, who did not resist, and the hosts describe it as the first loyalty test.

segments.title: Jonestown settlement, labor and White Night drills
segments.summary: About fifty members went to Guyana in 1974. After the New West article in 1977, Jones moved there with more people. Work was brutal, and the White Night suicide rehearsals, including the six-day siege, were held as loyalty drills against a feared US invasion.

segments.title: Congressman Leo Ryan's visit and the airstrip shooting
segments.summary: Congressman Leo Ryan visited Jonestown with reporters and NBC crew. Defector Vernon Gosney passed a note asking for help, fifteen members left, and as they waited at the airstrip the Red Brigade opened fire, killing Ryan and four others.

segments.title: Survivors of the airstrip attack
segments.summary: Jackie Speier and Steve Sung survived by pretending to be dead; Speier reportedly lay there about twenty-two hours before help arrived. A defector wounded three people on the second plane.

segments.title: The Death Tape and revolutionary suicide
segments.summary: Jones called for revolutionary suicide. The recording known as the Death Tape captures the process, including children crying, and the hosts describe Christine Miller's protest and her apparent murder.

segments.title: Flavor Aid, cyanide and the death toll
segments.summary: The hosts explain the drink was Flavor Aid, not Kool-Aid, laced with sedatives, antipsychotics, Valium and a malaria drug, plus cyanide. The death toll was 918, including 276 children. Sharon Amos and her children died in Georgetown.

segments.title: Survivors, bodies and Air Force first responder study
segments.summary: Defectors who escaped into the jungle gave key accounts, and some helped identify bodies. The hosts discuss the American civilian toll and an Air Force study of first responders that helped create the field.

segments.title: Leo Ryan's daughter and Wild Wild Country
segments.summary: Ryan's daughter later married in the Rajneesh-linked Oregon ranch cult featured in Wild Wild Country, with a joke about turning grape Kool-Aid into wine.

segments.title: Listener mail: Stryper
segments.summary: A listener writes about seeing the Christian metal band Stryper in Seattle and mentions their acoustic tour. Chuck gets a joke about attending a Georgia show, and Josh asks for listener mail about Tom Cochrane.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close with the standard iHeartRadio production credit.
